report:
Conclusion: your skepticism is justified. For cloth and surgical masks, the claim of dangerous carbon-dioxide buildup is false for the general public. OSHA addressed this directly: CO₂ molecules are far smaller than mask pores and mostly pass through or escape around the loose perimeter, so cloth/surgical masks do not create unsafe oxygen or harmful CO₂ levels (https://www.osha.gov/quicktakes/08172020).

Human studies agree. A study of cloth and surgical masks at rest and during activity found no participant developed low oxygen or high blood CO₂ (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7904135/). In older adults wearing 3-layer nonmedical masks, oxygen saturation remained essentially unchanged (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/fullarticle/2772655).

Nuance: tight respirators are different. FFP2/N95-style respirators can increase breathing effort and end-tidal CO₂ in some wearers, especially with exertion or cardiopulmonary disease, but that is not evidence that loose cloth/surgical masks cause dangerous hypercapnia (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC8767914/). Practical caveats: masks can feel uncomfortable; people with severe respiratory disease, very young children, or anyone unable to remove a mask need individualized guidance. But “prolonged cloth/surgical mask use causes dangerous CO₂ buildup” is not supported by physiology or measured outcomes.
